outputs.L1:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Michael Martin, Speaker of Britain’s House of Commons, announced Tuesday that he would resign amid widespread public anger over lawmakers’ expense claims.

Martin, whose statement lasted barely a minute, said he would step down on June 21. He is the first Speaker to be forced from office since 1695. Martin said he was resigning to promote “unity” in the House of Commons.

Later Tuesday, Prime Minister Gordon Brown announced recommendations for comprehensive reforms to the parliamentary expenses system, aimed at ending the “abuses and misjudgments of the past.” He proposed an independent panel to review expense claims from recent years, as well as the creation of an external agency to regulate reimbursements—an area Parliament currently oversees itself.

Parliament at “Westminster cannot operate like some gentlemen’s club,” Brown said. “There has got to be transparency. There has got to be a proper audit.”

The reforms remain proposals, and it is not yet clear whether they will be implemented. Brown also paid tribute to Martin and said he had chaired a meeting of party leaders Tuesday afternoon to discuss an overhaul of the expenses system.

The Speaker traditionally presides over debates and ensures parliamentary protocol is followed. However, MPs have focused much of their anger on Martin in part because his office also handles expense claims. Critics say he allowed claims to spiral out of control and failed to grasp the depth of public disgust over the sums being claimed—amounts that reached tens of thousands of dollars for some lawmakers.

Martin faced fierce criticism from MPs on Monday after addressing Parliament, with one lawmaker after another demanding to know when he would resign.

Politicians across the political spectrum have come under fire after weeks of front-page headlines revealing their expense claims. The claims included requests for reimbursements on mortgages that had already been paid off, members of the same family claiming the same expenses, and reimbursements for lavish home furnishings.

Justice Minister Shahid Malik resigned from the Cabinet over his claims, which he insisted were within allowable limits. The governing Labour Party also cut ties with MP Elliot Morley, a former Cabinet minister, over his expense claims.

The expenses scandal emerged through a series of recent front-page reports in The Daily Telegraph. The expense claims had been scheduled for public release in the summer, but the newspaper obtained them early. Many lawmakers highlighted by the Telegraph have insisted they broke no rules.

Shortly before Martin’s resignation, London’s Metropolitan Police announced they would not investigate the leaking of the expense reports to the press. “The leak of documents is not something that the [Metropolitan Police] would condone,” the force said in a statement, but added that it believed it was unlikely to obtain the evidence needed to bring a successful prosecution.

The police had not yet decided whether to investigate whether politicians broke the law through their expense claims, the statement added.

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Michael Martin announced Tuesday he will resign as Speaker of the British House of Commons, becoming the highest-profile political casualty of a widening scandal over lawmakers’ expense claims that has shaken public confidence in Parliament.

Martin told MPs he would step down on June 21, a brief statement that followed days of mounting pressure from lawmakers across party lines. His departure makes him the first Speaker in more than 300 years to be effectively forced from office.

“In order that unity can be maintained, I have decided that I will relinquish the office of Speaker on Sunday, June 21,” Martin said in the chamber. “This will allow the House to proceed to elect a new Speaker on Monday, June 22.”

The announcement came amid public anger over revelations that Members of Parliament had used taxpayer-funded allowances to claim reimbursements for items ranging from home renovations and furnishings to gardening work and mortgage payments. The scandal erupted after The Daily Telegraph began publishing details of MPs’ expenses, exposing practices that, while in some cases within parliamentary rules, were widely viewed as excessive or inappropriate.

Martin had faced criticism not only over the expenses system itself, but also over his handling of the crisis. Opponents accused him of being too slow to recognize the seriousness of the scandal and too focused on investigating how the expense records were leaked rather than on reforming the system. In an extraordinary move, a group of MPs signed a motion of no confidence in the Speaker — a rare challenge to an office traditionally treated as above partisan conflict.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown, whose Labour government was already under political strain, said Parliament had to respond with sweeping reforms to restore trust.

Brown proposed changes including tougher independent oversight of MPs’ expenses, clearer rules on second-home allowances, greater transparency in claims, and stronger disciplinary procedures for lawmakers found to have abused the system. He also backed moving responsibility for MPs’ pay and allowances away from Parliament and toward an independent authority.

“The old system has lost public confidence,” Brown said in comments outlining the need for reform. “We must make changes that are clear, tough and independently enforced.”

The controversy has affected all major parties. Several MPs said they would repay questionable claims, while others announced they would stand down at the next general election. Party leaders moved quickly to distance themselves from the most damaging revelations, ordering internal reviews and demanding repayments where claims were deemed unacceptable.

Among the claims reported were reimbursements for cleaning, furniture, repairs, and in some cases costs connected to properties designated as second homes. Critics said the system encouraged MPs to maximize allowances with too little scrutiny, while defenders argued that Parliament had long operated under vague and outdated rules.

Martin, a Labour MP from Glasgow before becoming Speaker in 2000, was responsible for maintaining order in the Commons and representing the authority of Parliament. The Speaker is expected to be politically neutral once elected to the role. But in recent weeks, Martin’s position became increasingly untenable as MPs argued that only new leadership could help Parliament regain credibility.

His resignation marks a dramatic moment in British political history. The last Speaker to be removed under comparable pressure was Sir John Trevor in 1695, after a corruption scandal.

The House of Commons is now expected to elect a new Speaker tasked with guiding Parliament through one of its most serious crises in modern times. But Martin’s departure is unlikely to end the scandal, as pressure grows for broader constitutional and ethical reforms — and as voters demand accountability from MPs who approved and benefited from a system now widely seen as broken.

## The 2009 UK Parliamentary Expenses Scandal: Michael Martin’s Fall and a Crisis of Trust

The 2009 UK parliamentary expenses scandal became one of the most damaging political crises in modern British history, exposing widespread misuse of allowances by MPs and triggering public anger at Westminster. At the centre of the storm was Michael Martin, the Speaker of the House of Commons, who was forced to announce that he would step down after fierce criticism from MPs over his handling of the affair.

The scandal erupted after *The Daily Telegraph* obtained and began publishing leaked details of MPs’ expenses claims in May 2009. The revelations showed that many MPs had claimed public money for questionable items, second homes, mortgage arrangements, furnishings, repairs, and other personal costs. Although some claims were within the rules, the disclosures suggested that the expenses system had become deeply flawed and overly generous, with MPs able to benefit from weak oversight and opaque procedures.

Among the most notorious claims reported were expenses for home improvements, gardening, cleaning, and luxury fittings, as well as symbolic examples such as claims linked to a duck house and a moat. The stories caused outrage because they emerged during a period of economic difficulty, when many members of the public were facing financial pressure.

Michael Martin, who had been Speaker since 2000, came under intense pressure as MPs from across the political spectrum accused him of failing to respond adequately to the scandal. Critics argued that he had been too defensive of the existing expenses system and too slow to accept the need for radical reform. Martin was also criticised for appearing to rebuke MPs who raised the issue in the Commons, rather than acknowledging the scale of public anger.

The pressure culminated in an extraordinary confrontation in the House of Commons. Several MPs openly challenged his authority, a rare and dramatic development given the Speaker’s traditionally respected and impartial role. Martin’s position became untenable, and on 19 May 2009 he announced that he would resign as Speaker. His departure made him the first Speaker in more than 300 years to be effectively forced from office. He formally stepped down in June 2009.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown responded to the scandal by promising reforms to restore confidence in Parliament. He acknowledged public anger and supported moves toward greater transparency and independent oversight of MPs’ expenses. The crisis led to the creation of the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority, designed to take control of MPs’ pay and expenses away from Parliament itself.

The role of *The Daily Telegraph* was decisive. Its leaks transformed what had been a long-running dispute over transparency into a full-scale political scandal. Before the newspaper’s publication of the files, campaigners and journalists had spent years pressing for disclosure under freedom of information laws. The Telegraph’s reporting revealed the scale and detail of the claims in a way that official publication had not yet done, forcing rapid resignations, repayments, disciplinary action, and eventually wider reform.

The scandal damaged all major parties and contributed to a collapse in public trust in MPs. Several politicians stood down at the 2010 general election, while others faced investigations or repayment demands. More broadly, the affair became a symbol of Westminster’s perceived arrogance and detachment from ordinary voters.

Michael Martin’s resignation marked the most visible institutional casualty of the scandal, but the deeper impact was on Parliament itself. The expenses affair exposed serious weaknesses in self-regulation and demonstrated the power of media leaks to force accountability. It remains a defining episode in debates about political ethics, transparency, and public trust in British democracy.

**Breaking news report — Westminster expenses scandal: Speaker Michael Martin to resign**

**London, May 2009** — Michael Martin, the Speaker of the House of Commons, has announced that he will step down, becoming the first Commons Speaker in more than 300 years to be forced from office amid a political crisis. His resignation follows days of mounting anger over the parliamentary expenses scandal, which has engulfed MPs from all major parties and shaken public confidence in Westminster.

Martin told MPs in a brief statement that he would relinquish the speakership on **21 June 2009**, triggering the election of a new Speaker. His departure comes after a dramatic breakdown in support among backbench MPs, many of whom blamed him for the Commons’ slow, defensive response to revelations about MPs’ expense claims.

## Why the Speaker was under pressure

Although the Speaker does not personally approve every individual MP’s expenses claim, the office is central to the Commons administration and has significant influence over the system governing MPs’ allowances.

As Speaker, Martin chaired or was closely associated with Commons bodies responsible for oversight of parliamentary administration, including the structures linked to Members’ allowances and the Fees Office. Critics accused the Commons leadership under Martin of presiding over a culture of secrecy, resisting transparency, and failing to reform an expenses regime that allowed MPs to claim large sums with limited public scrutiny.

Martin had already faced criticism before the latest disclosures for the Commons’ handling of **Freedom of Information** requests seeking publication of MPs’ expenses. Parliamentary authorities fought a long legal battle to prevent detailed claims from being released. When the information was eventually due to come out officially, the scandal exploded first through leaked documents published by *The Daily Telegraph*.

The Speaker was also criticised for appearing more concerned with how the leak occurred than with the substance of the abuses. In a tense Commons session, he rebuked MPs who raised points of order about reform and investigation, further fuelling the impression that the parliamentary establishment was trying to protect itself.

## Examples of abuses and controversial claims

The expenses scandal revealed a wide range of claims by MPs for second homes, household goods, renovations, mortgage payments and other costs. Some claims were within the rules as written but were widely viewed as morally indefensible; others raised questions about whether rules had been breached.

Prominent examples reported during the scandal included:

- **Second-home “flipping”**: MPs were accused of switching the designation of their “main” and “second” homes, allowing them to claim expenses on different properties and, in some cases, reduce tax liabilities or maximise allowances.

- **Mortgage claims**: Some MPs claimed for mortgage interest on second homes, with questions raised in certain cases about whether mortgages had been paid off or whether claims were properly supported.

- **Luxury and unusual household items**: Claims included expensive furniture, televisions, kitchen equipment, gardening, and other domestic costs that many voters regarded as excessive.

- **Moat cleaning**: Conservative MP **Douglas Hogg** was widely reported to have claimed costs associated with maintaining his country estate, including a claim linked to cleaning a moat. He denied wrongdoing but announced he would stand down at the next election.

- **Duck house**: Conservative MP **Sir Peter Viggers** was reported to have claimed for a floating duck island for his pond. The claim became one of the most notorious symbols of the scandal; he later said he would leave Parliament.

- **Home improvements and renovations**: MPs across parties were reported to have claimed for repairs, decorating, appliances, bathroom work, and other improvements to properties designated as second homes.

- **Capital gains and property arrangements**: Some MPs faced questions over whether they had benefited financially by designating homes one way for expenses and another way for tax purposes.

The revelations cut across party lines, damaging Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats and smaller parties. Party leaders rushed to order repayments, suspend MPs from party positions, and promise tougher oversight.

## Why Martin’s resignation is historic

The Speaker is traditionally expected to be politically neutral and is normally treated with considerable deference by MPs. For a Speaker to be forced out is extraordinarily rare. Martin’s resignation is widely described as the first such departure since **Sir John Trevor in 1695**, who was removed after a bribery scandal.

Martin, a former Labour MP for Glasgow North East, had held the speakership since 2000. His supporters argued he was being unfairly made the scapegoat for a system that MPs of all parties had used for years. But critics said the Speaker had failed to grasp the scale of public fury and had been too closely identified with efforts to keep expenses secret.

## Would police investigate?

At the time of Martin’s resignation, the key question was whether any MPs’ conduct would cross the line from unethical or embarrassing into potentially criminal behaviour.

Police were under pressure to examine the most serious cases, particularly where there were allegations of false accounting, fraud, or claims for costs that were not actually incurred. However, authorities were cautious about launching a broad criminal inquiry into the entire expenses system, because many controversial claims may have been permitted under Commons rules even if they appeared abusive to the public.

The likely approach was case-by-case assessment. Police would be expected to investigate only where there was evidence suggesting deliberate dishonesty, such as knowingly false claims, forged documentation, or claims for non-existent expenses.

In the months following the scandal, police and prosecutors did examine a number of cases, and several parliamentarians were later charged and convicted over expenses-related offences. But Martin’s resignation itself was primarily a political and constitutional event, not a criminal finding against him personally.

## Wider impact

Martin’s departure intensified demands for sweeping reform of parliamentary expenses. Proposals included removing MPs from direct control over their own allowances, creating an independent regulator, publishing claims in full, banning questionable second-home practices, and tightening rules around mortgages, rent, family members and property designations.

The scandal has become one of the gravest crises for Parliament in modern times. Martin’s resignation is intended to draw a line under the Commons’ handling of the affair, but public anger suggests the political fallout is far from over.
